instruction: Independent recheck after targeted board-language audit. Inspect every question against the complete current composed scene. For exp26b-u13-002, treat the rim as a completed past action and check only present-tense contradictions; for exp26-u13-021 and exp26-u13-025, verify current side-board wording against puck and player geometry. Confirm actor references, answer contracts and exact hashes. Do not edit the bank.

scenarios.title: Find the middle hinge after the rim
scenarios.objective: Use the middle hinge to connect a rim without skating into the carrier’s lane
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. D1 retrieved a rim at the left corner. YOU is low middle, D2 is higher, and Gold 1 steers the carrier toward the wall.
cues: D1 owns the puck in the left corner.
YOU are low middle; D2 is higher behind the play.

questions.prompt: Which player has the puck?
questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to D1, so YOU’s job is support; if possession changes, the support read resets.

questions.prompt: Which two details make YOU a useful hinge?

options.text: A visible lane between D1 and D2
Distance that keeps you available below pressure

questions.explanation: A separated middle lane connects the defenders and leaves D1 room to carry; standing on D1’s route removes the support option.

questions.prompt: Order one hinge-support read.
questions.explanation: Pressure determines room; showing the lane gives a second outlet; a closed lane requires a new angle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into an example hinge lane inside Gold 1 and clear of D1’s puck route.
questions.explanation: The inside spot gives D1 a short connection without copying the corner route; if Gold 1 cuts inside, widen or drop to keep a lane.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 steps into the middle lane, what is a useful change?

options.text: Slide to a new support angle while D1 protects the puck
Stay hidden behind Gold 1 and call for a pass

questions.explanation: Gold 1 removes the original hinge, so changing angle preserves an outlet; if the middle reopens, return without crowding D1.

questions.prompt: How does your support help D1 even when D1 does not pass?
questions.explanation: A visible hinge makes Gold 1 respect a second lane, giving D1 time to carry or connect to D2; if pressure ignores you, D1 can use the space.

scenarios.title: Remain useful higher than the board battle
scenarios.objective: Recognize high support while teammates contest the puck low.
scenarios.briefing: F1 and Gold 1 contest a loose puck along the attacking-zone side boards. F2 is closer to Gold’s net than they are. YOU are the high forward; this exercise assigns YOU to support higher than the battle until control changes. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: What is the puck state at the board battle?
questions.explanation: The puck marker is separate from F1 and Gold 1, as the briefing states.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs could high support serve?

options.text: Guaranteed possession merely by standing high
Help against a counterattack if Gold wins
An outlet if Navy wins control

questions.explanation: High support can preserve options in either outcome, but does not win the battle itself.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read from high support behind the battle.

options.text: Check the high-slot space and opposing outlet

questions.explanation: The high role is this exercise’s stated plan; a coach may assign a different forecheck elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a useful high-slot support example without joining the scrum.
questions.explanation: The reference keeps separation from the wall contest and access to middle ice. Other distances may suit the play.

questions.prompt: If F1 wins clean possession and looks inside, what could you offer?

options.text: An automatic move into F1’s crowded wall space
A claim that the puck remains loose

questions.explanation: Control permits an attacking read, but you still need a reachable lane.

questions.prompt: Explain why the high forward’s position matters before the battle is decided.
questions.explanation: Describe both the possible outlet and defensive recovery roles, using the opponent’s location.

questions.prompt: Which Navy player is assigned the high support role?
questions.explanation: YOU is the assigned high Navy forward supporting above the loose-puck battle; if F1 wins, offer the high outlet, while a Gold win changes YOU to recovery.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs can high support serve?

options.text: Be a reset if F1 wins it
Recover inside if Gold wins it

questions.explanation: High separation supports either possession outcome; joining the battle removes balance.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly higher and inside, above the board battle.
questions.explanation: The high-inside position keeps both puck outcomes visible and protects the middle; if F1 wins cleanly, lower into the next support lane.

questions.prompt: Why should high support remain useful before the battle is decided?
questions.explanation: Ownership is unknown, so a balanced position can attack or recover without guessing; once control is clear, move to the new job.

scenarios.title: Follow the assigned faceoff support role
scenarios.objective: Use a simple stated retrieval plan without treating it as a universal system.
scenarios.briefing: This even-strength practice draw has already occurred. The coach asked YOU, the winger, to pursue a loose puck toward the side boards while C stays inside. The puck remains loose; no faceoff violation is being assessed. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: Which task did the coach assign YOU after the draw?

options.text: Pursue the loose puck near the side boards

questions.explanation: The assignment is explicitly stated and applies only to this exercise.

questions.prompt: Which two facts should update that plan?

options.text: Whether C’s inside support remains available
The assumption that all faceoffs use this arrangement

questions.explanation: A planned role still responds to possession and support.

questions.prompt: Arrange one follow-up to this draw.

options.text: Check the opponent and assigned support
Pursue or adjust to the actual control

questions.explanation: The sequence is a suggested response under the stated drill plan, not a universal faceoff play.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward an example retrieval position near the side boards.
questions.explanation: This follows the stated role without moving onto C. Actual reach and timing remain unvalidated.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 controls the puck before you arrive, what should you do?

options.text: Act as if the draw was already won by Navy
Follow the retrieval route with no new read

questions.explanation: The opponent’s control changes the action even when the pre-draw plan was clear.

questions.prompt: Why does knowing a faceoff plan not remove the need to read the puck?
questions.explanation: A plan assigns starting responsibilities; the bounce, opponent and possession decide what is possible next.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate should YOU keep inside as you pursue the loose puck?
questions.explanation: C is the Navy teammate assigned to stay inside, so YOU can pursue toward the boards without losing the middle; if Gold 1 controls first, recover instead of completing the old route.

questions.prompt: Which two facts should update that faceoff plan?

options.text: The faceoff was in the previous period

questions.explanation: Loose ownership and Gold 1’s route decide whether pursuit remains useful; period history does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the side-board puck while keeping C’s inside lane visible.
questions.explanation: The board-side route follows the assignment and leaves C inside; if Gold reaches the puck, stop the chase and support coverage.

questions.prompt: Why does a faceoff plan still require a puck read?
questions.explanation: The plan describes an intended first job, but the loose puck and opponent route can change ownership; if Gold wins it, recover instead of completing the old route.
